data.q: Which .NET CLI tool is used to collect CPU sampling traces from a running .NET application?
data.e: dotnet-trace collects performance traces (CPU sampling, GC events, etc.) via EventPipe. dotnet-counters is for metrics, dotnet-dump for heap dumps, dotnet-gcdump for GC heap dumps.

data.q: What does the `dotnet-counters monitor` command display by default?
o: CPU usage, GC heap size, Gen 0/1/2 collections, ThreadPool queue length, and exception count
Only CPU usage and memory allocation rate
data.e: dotnet-counters monitor shows a default set of counters including CPU, GC heap size, generation collection counts, ThreadPool stats, and exceptions. You can specify custom providers with `--counters`.

data.q: Which tool is specifically designed to capture a snapshot of the GC heap for offline analysis of memory leaks?
data.e: dotnet-gcdump creates a portable GC heap dump (`.gcdump`) optimized for heap analysis (object counts, sizes, roots). dotnet-dump creates a full core dump (OS-specific).

data.q: When analyzing a `dotnet-trace` file in PerfView or speedscope, what does the "GC" event provider primarily reveal?
o: Garbage collection pauses, generations, heap sizes, and allocation rates
data.e: The GC provider in EventPipe emits events for GC start/stop, generation, heap size before/after, allocation tick, and more — essential for diagnosing GC pressure and pause times.

data.q: What is the primary purpose of `dotnet-dump collect`?
o: Capture a full process core dump (including native and managed heap) for debugging crashes or hangs
Export GC heap as a portable format
data.e: dotnet-dump creates a full memory dump (core dump on Linux/macOS, minidump on Windows) suitable for SOS/lldb debugging of crashes, hangs, or memory issues. It is OS-specific and larger than .gcdump.

data.q: Which .NET tool enables attaching to a running process without stopping it to collect a trace or dump?
data.e: All three tools (dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters, dotnet-dump) can attach to a running process by PID via `--process-id` without pausing it. dotnet-gcdump also supports this.

data.q: In BenchmarkDotNet, what does the `[MemoryDiagnoser]` attribute enable?
o: Measures CPU cycles and branch mispredictions
Reports allocated bytes, Gen 0/1/2 collections, and working set per benchmark
Profiles GC pause times via ETW
data.e: [MemoryDiagnoser] uses EventPipe to report allocation rate, Gen 0/1/2 collection counts, and memory usage per iteration. It is the standard way to benchmark allocations in .NET.

data.q: What is `dotnet-monitor` primarily used for in production environments?
o: Real-time CPU profiling via a web API
A sidecar/daemon that exposes REST APIs to collect traces, dumps, gcdumps, and metrics on demand
data.e: dotnet-monitor runs as a sidecar or daemon, exposing HTTP endpoints to trigger dotnet-trace, dotnet-dump, dotnet-gcdump, and dotnet-counters on running apps — ideal for Kubernetes/production diagnostics.

data.q: Which ETW provider name is used by the .NET runtime for GC events in EventPipe?
data.e: The .NET runtime ETW provider is `Microsoft-Windows-DotNETRuntime` (GUID: e13c0d23-ccbc-4e12-931b-d9cc2eee27e4). In EventPipe, it's exposed as `Microsoft-Windows-DotNETRuntime` with keywords for GC, JIT, Threading, etc.

data.q: When using `dotnet-trace collect --format speedscope`, what is the output file extension and primary use case?
o: .speedscope - view in speedscope.app for interactive flame graphs
.json - raw event data for custom parsing
data.e: `--format speedscope` outputs a `.speedscope.json` file compatible with speedscope.app, a web-based flame graph viewer. The default `--format nettrace` is for PerfView/Visual Studio.

data.q: What does the `ThreadPool` counter `Queue Length` indicate when observed via `dotnet-counters`?
o: Number of work items waiting for an available thread
data.e: ThreadPool Queue Length = work items queued but not yet executing. A consistently high value indicates thread pool starvation or blocking work on ThreadPool threads.

data.q: Which Visual Studio Diagnostic Tool window allows you to take heap snapshots and compare them to find memory leaks during a debug session?
data.e: The Memory Profiler (part of Performance Profiler, Alt+F2) lets you take snapshots of the managed heap, compare them, and view object counts/sizes/roots to identify leaks. The Diagnostic Tools window shows events and memory usage graph but not detailed heap diff.

data.q: What is the effect of setting the environment variable `COMPlus_GCServer=1`?
o: Enables Workstation GC with concurrent collections
Enables Server GC (multiple heaps, one per logical CPU)
data.e: COMPlus_GCServer=1 (or `<ServerGarbageCollection>true</ServerGarbageCollection>` in .csproj) enables Server GC: multiple heaps, dedicated GC threads, better throughput for server workloads. Default is Workstation GC.

data.q: In a `dotnet-trace` flame graph, what does a wide, flat plateau at the top typically represent?
o: High CPU utilization in a single method
GC suspension (threads blocked at a safepoint during GC)
data.e: A flat, wide top in a flame graph often indicates threads are stopped at a GC safepoint (GC suspension). All threads pause, so the stack is identical across threads, creating a plateau. Lock contention shows as narrow towers; CPU work shows as varied stacks.

data.q: Which command exports a `dotnet-trace` file to a human-readable text summary of GC stats?
data.e: `dotnet-trace gcstats <trace-file>` outputs a summary of GC events: pause times, generations, heap sizes, allocation rates. It's a quick way to assess GC health without opening PerfView.

data.q: What is the recommended way to diagnose high CPU usage in a containerized .NET 8 app running in Kubernetes?
o: SSH into the container and run `top`
Use `dotnet-monitor` sidecar and call `/trace/start` via HTTP to collect a `dotnet-trace` profile
Restart the pod with `dotnet-counters` logging to stdout
data.e: dotnet-monitor as a sidecar is the production-standard approach: it exposes REST endpoints to start/stop traces, dumps, and counters without SSH or code changes. Works in Kubernetes, Cloud Run, etc.
